title: Find direction with the sun and a stick (shadow-tip method)
asks: how to find north with a stick and the sun
which way is north no compass daytime
how to tell east and west from a shadow
lost my compass how do i find north
how 2 find north with a stik
no compass but the sun is out, how do we get our direction, over
answer: Place a stick or branch into the ground at a level spot where it casts a distinct shadow. Mark the tip of the shadow with a stone, twig or other means. This first mark is always the west mark.
Wait 10 to 15 minutes, until the shadow tip has moved a few inches. Mark the new position of the shadow tip in the same way.
Draw a straight line through the two marks. This is an approximate east-west line.
Stand with the first mark (west) to your left. North is to your front, east is to your right and south is to your rear.
A line drawn at right angles to the east-west line, at any point, is an approximate north-south line.
The stick does not have to be vertical, and a flat spot the size of your hand is enough. The shadow tip of any stationary object, such as the end of a tree limb, serves just as well.

Why it works: the sun rises in the east and sets in the west (but rarely due east and due west), and the shadow tip moves in just the opposite direction. So the first mark is always west and the second mark east, any place on earth.

At local noon: north of 23.4 degrees north latitude the shadow points north; south of 23.4 degrees south latitude it points south. In the tropics the sun can be either north or south at noon, but the shadow still moves toward the east.

To tell the time with a shadow clock: set the stick vertically in the ground where the east-west line and the north-south line cross. The west part of the east-west line is 0600 and the east part is 1800. The north-south line is the noon line, and the shadow of the stick is the hour hand.
warnings: The shadow-tip method gives approximate directions, and is not effective beyond about 66 degrees of latitude in either hemisphere.
The shadow clock always reads 0600 at sunrise and 1800 at sunset. It is closest to conventional clock time at midday; the spacing of the other hours varies somewhat with the locality and date.
Do not rely on one form of navigation. (The Army cold-weather manual gives this note for movement in extremely cold weather.)

quotes.text: Step 1. Place a stick or branch into the ground at a level spot where a distinct shadow will be cast. Mark the shadow tip with a stone, twig, or other means. This first shadow mark is always the West direction.

The sun "rises in the east and sets in the west" (but rarely due east and due west). The shadow tip moves in just the opposite direction. Therefore, the first shadow-tip mark is always in the west direction, and the second mark in the east direction, any place on earth.
Step 2. Wait 10 to 15 minutes until the shadow tip moves a few inches. Mark the new position of the shadow tip in the same way as the first.
Step 3. Draw a straight line through the two marks to obtain an approximate east-west line.
Step 4. Standing with the first mark (west) to your left, the other directions are simple; north is to the front, east is to the right, and south is to the rear.
Note: A line drawn at right angles to the east-west line at any point forms the same approximate north-south line, which will help orient a person to the same cardinal directions.
Inclining the stick to obtain a more convenient shadow does not impair the accuracy of the shadow-tip method.
A flat spot, the size of the hand, is all that is necessary for shadow-tip markings and the base of the stick can be either above, below, or to one side of it.
In addition, any stationary object (the end of a tree limb or the notch where branches are jointed) serves just as well as an implanted stick because only the shadow tip is marked.
The shadow-tip method is ineffective for use beyond 66'/2° latitude in either hemisphere due to the position of the sun above the horizon.

North of 23.4°N, the sun is always due south at local noon and the shadow points north. South of 23.4°S, the sun is always due north at local noon and the shadow points south. In the tropics, the sun can be either north or south at noon, depending on the date and location, but the shadow progresses to the east regardless of the date. This method consists of four basic steps
Move the stick to the intersection of the east-west line and the north-south line, and set it vertically in the ground.
The west part of the east-west line indicates the time is 0600 and the east part is 1800.
The north-south line now becomes the noon line. The shadow of the stick is the hour hand in the shadow clock

The shadow clock is not a timepiece in the ordinary sense. It always reads 0600 at sunrise and 1800 at sunset. However, it does provide a satisfactory means of telling time in the absence of properly set watches.
Shadow-clock time is closest to conventional clock time at midday, but the spacing of the other hours, compared to conventional time, varies somewhat with the locality and date.
Do not rely on one form of navigation when moving in extremely cold weather.

conflict: Noon shadow: TC 21-3 (2025) para 6-34 says 'At noon in the northern hemisphere, shadows fall to the north of objects', and ATP 3-50.21 (2018) para 7-21 says shadows 'will point north at noon' in the Northern Hemisphere; ATP 3-50.21 para 7-22 is more specific: only north of 23.4 degrees N is the noon shadow always to the north, and in the tropics the sun can be either north or south at noon. The card uses the more specific statement.
